meta.ogDescription: Widely credited to Casey Stengel, unrecorded in his lifetime. Earliest printing found: a 1982 anthology — and one 2010 book credits Bill Veeck instead.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1890–1975 · Hall of Fame baseball manager, New York Yankees and New York Mets
answer.sourceLine: The line is credited to Stengel in Stengel-specific quotation collections, and the earliest printing we could locate — Kevin Nelson’s Baseball’s Greatest Quotes (Simon and Schuster, 1982) — already puts it in his mouth, alongside his own Senate-testimony riff. But nothing from Stengel’s lifetime records him saying it: no date, no ballpark, no interview, no newspaper report.

source.excerpt: “Without losers,” he philosophized, “where would the winners be?”
trail: Wikiquote lists the line among Casey Stengel’s quotes and sources it to The Gospel According to Casey (1992), ed. Berkow & Kaplan, St. Martin’s Press, p. 19, as cited in The Executive’s Book of Quotations (1994), ed. Martin & Moskin, Oxford University Press, p. 299 — see the entry ↗. The page has no “Disputed” or “Misattributed” section.

Both of those books are late. The earliest printing we could locate is a decade older: Kevin Nelson’s Baseball’s Greatest Quotes (Simon and Schuster, 1982), scanned at the Internet Archive ↗ — still after Stengel’s death in 1975.
A full-text search of the Internet Archive’s scanned books ↗ returns no printing of the phrase earlier than that 1982 anthology, in any attribution.

Quote Investigator has no article on this quote, so there is no specialist tracing to defer to — the strongest documented claim available is “printed as Stengel’s from 1982,” not “said by Stengel on a known day.”
source.excerptNote: As the line reads in Kevin Nelson’s Baseball’s Greatest Quotes (1982), where it sits beside Stengel’s celebrated Senate-testimony riff — “I became a major league manager in several cities and was discharged. We call it discharged…” — in a run of his own quotations. The bare form “Without losers, where would the winners be?” is what later collections print.
source.rightsNote: No original utterance or first publication can be established, so no copyright status can be asserted for the sentence itself. What is certain is that it is not in the public domain by age: Stengel lived from 1890 to 1975, and every located printing — the 1982 Nelson anthology, the 1992 Gospel According to Casey, the 1994 Executive’s Book of Quotations — falls well after 1931. Those individual editions remain in copyright to their own publishers and compilers.

author.name: Casey Stengel
author.heading: About Casey Stengel
author.metaLine: 1890–1975 · Baseball manager · New York Yankees and New York Mets
author.bio: Charles Dillon “Casey” Stengel won ten pennants and seven World Series managing the New York Yankees from 1949 to 1960, then took charge of the expansion New York Mets from 1962 to 1965 — a team that lost 120 games in its first season, a twentieth-century record for futility. His circular, clause-piling way of talking was famous enough to earn its own name, Stengelese, and he was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1966. That reputation as baseball’s great wit is exactly why lines drift toward him: a good one-sentence gag about losing sounds like Stengel whether or not he ever said it.

misattribution.heading: What the credit actually rests on
misattribution.intro: Nobody has shown this line is wrong. What is missing is the other half — any record of Stengel saying it. Every printing we could find postdates his death in 1975, and the credit travels without an occasion attached.

items.why: No speech, interview, newspaper report, book or broadcast from Stengel’s lifetime has been tied to this sentence. A full-text search of the Internet Archive’s scanned books ↗ surfaces the phrase only in printings from 1982 onward.

Peter Handrinos’s The Funniest Baseball Book Ever (Andrews McMeel, 2010) prints the identical sentence and credits it to the club owner Bill Veeck, not Stengel — see the scanned edition ↗. No earlier Veeck source supports it either, so this reads as drift rather than a correction.

Encyclopedia.com’s Stengel entry prints the line with no citation at all ↗, pairing it with his “only thing worse than a Mets game” crack. That is the usual pattern: the quote is repeated, the sourcing never is.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest verdict: the credit to Stengel is old, consistent and plausible — the 1982 anthology that first prints it ↗ already sets it among his own lines — but it is a credit, not a record. Until a source from his lifetime turns up, this stays attributed rather than verified.

context.heading: Why it sounds exactly like him
lead: Stengel took over the New York Mets in 1962, their first season, and the team lost 120 games — a twentieth-century record. He managed them through 1965, and his job in those years was less about winning than about selling the loss: turning a hopeless expansion club into something New York could love. A one-line shrug that reframes losing as a public service is precisely the register he worked in.

That is also the trap. A quip this well-fitted to a man’s legend is the kind that attaches to him whether or not he coined it — and in this case the attribution shows up only in anthologies compiled after his death, never in a contemporaneous report.
context.detailsSummary: What we searched, and what we did not find
detailsBody: A full-text search of the Internet Archive’s scanned-book corpus for the exact phrase returns printings only from 1982 onward. Nothing in it predates Stengel’s death in 1975.

Quote Investigator has no article on this line, and Wikiquote’s Casey Stengel page carries no “Disputed” or “Misattributed” section at all — so there is no specialist finding to defer to in either direction. The absence of a debunking is not evidence the quote is genuine; it means nobody has traced it.

No newspaper archive we could reach returned a period printing. Several archives — HathiTrust, the Google Books API, and per-item search inside restricted archive.org scans — refused access rather than returning nothing, so their silence is not evidence either.
context.pull: A line that fits the legend too well is a line worth checking.

Casey Stengel was born 30 July 1890 and died 29 September 1975; he managed the New York Mets from 1962 to 1965, and the 1962 Mets lost 120 games, a twentieth-century futility record. His way of talking became known as Stengelese.
Charles Dillon "Casey" Stengel, nicknamed The Ol' Perfessor, was born 30 July 1890, died 29 September 1975, managed the New York Mets 1962-1965, and was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1966.
